title: Read N Characters Given read4 II - Call Multiple Times
statement:
A text file can only be reached through a helper `read4(buf4)`. Each call to it copies the next (at most) 4 characters of the file into the array `buf4`, starting at index 0, moves the helper's own position in the file past them, and returns how many characters it copied. Near the end of the file that count is below 4, and once the file is used up it is 0.

Using only `read4`, build a reader `(buf, n)` that copies the next `n` characters of the file into `buf`, starting at index 0, and returns how many it copied; the count is smaller than `n` only when the file runs out. The reader is called several times on the same file, and every call must continue exactly where the previous call stopped, so characters that `read4` already delivered but an earlier call did not need must not be lost. `buf` always has room for `n` characters.

Write `read(read4)`: it receives the `read4` helper and returns the reader function `(buf, n) => count`. Each case is written as `[file, queries]`: the file's text, which your code never sees directly, and the `n` of each successive reader call. The result lists, for each call, the characters it placed in `buf` (`buf[0..count-1]` joined into a string).
constraints: file contains only English letters and digits
notes:
## Intuition

`read4` always hands over characters in blocks of 4, but callers ask for any `n`. When a request ends in the middle of a block, the rest of that block has already left the file and `read4` will never return it again. So the reader must keep those leftovers and serve them first on the next call. A 4-slot array plus two indices is enough: `buf4` holds the last block, `start` points at its first unused character and `end` is how many characters it holds. (A simpler but wasteful idea is to keep every delivered character in a growing queue and take from its front.)

## Approach

1. `read(read4)` creates `buf4`, `start = 0` and `end = 0`. They live in the closure, so they survive between reader calls.
2. The reader counts `copied` characters and loops while `copied < n`.
3. When the block is used up (`start === end`), refill it with `end = read4(buf4)` and reset `start` to 0.
4. If the refill returned 0, the file is finished: stop early.
5. Otherwise copy `buf4[start]` into `buf[copied]` and advance both indices.
6. Return `copied`.

## Example 1, step by step

The file is `"abc"` and the calls ask for 1, 2 and 1 characters.

- Call 1 (`n = 1`): the block is empty, so `read4` fills `buf4` with `a b c` and returns 3 (`end = 3`). Copy `a`; `start = 1`, `copied = 1`. Result `"a"`.
- Call 2 (`n = 2`): `start = 1 < end = 3`, so no `read4` is needed. Copy `b` and `c`; `start = 3`. Result `"bc"`.
- Call 3 (`n = 1`): `start === end`, so `read4` runs and returns 0. The loop stops with `copied = 0`. Result `""`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) per call: each character is copied once into `buf4` and once into `buf`, and `read4` runs at most about n / 4 + 1 times.
- Space: O(1): only the 4-slot block and two indices are kept.

## Pitfalls

- Reading with `read4` straight into `buf` (the single-call version of this problem) throws away the tail of the last block, so the next call skips characters.
- Refill only when the block is empty; calling `read4` early jumps ahead in the file.
- Stop as soon as `read4` returns 0, or the loop never ends on a short file.
- Keep the state inside the closure, not in globals, so each file gets its own reader.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `buf4` | the latest block of up to 4 characters from `read4` |
| `start` | index of the next unused character in `buf4` |
| `end` | number of valid characters in `buf4` |
| `buf`, `n` | the caller's destination and how many characters it wants |
| `copied` | characters placed in `buf` during this call |

narration.2: A 4-slot block that keeps characters read4 delivered but no call has used yet.
narration.3: start points at the next unused character of the block.
narration.4: end is how many characters the block holds; 0 means it is empty.
narration.6: Return the reader; the closure keeps buf4, start and end between calls.
narration.7: Count the characters this call has copied.
narration.8: Keep going until the caller has n characters.
narration.9: The block is used up, so it must be refilled.
narration.10: Ask read4 for the next block; it reports how many characters arrived.
narration.11: Start reading the new block from its first slot.
narration.12: read4 returned nothing: the file is finished.
narration.13: Stop early with fewer than n characters.
narration.16: Hand over the next unused character from the block.
narration.17: One more character delivered to the caller.
narration.18: Move past the character just used.
narration.20: Report how many characters this call delivered.
